screens.title: Your cat is part of a food chain
lines: When your cat pounces on a sparrow in the backyard, she's the top of a food chain you can watch from the window.
That sparrow ate caterpillars, the caterpillars ate the rosebush, and the rosebush ate sunlight. Energy is on the move.

vocab.meaning: a living thing that makes its own food from sunlight, like a plant
a living thing that gets energy by eating other living things
a path showing who eats whom, with energy passing along it

screens.framing: No grade, no pressure — just explore. Even a guess teaches your brain what to notice.

screens.title: Waves carry energy, not stuff
lines: Pluck a tight strand of knitting yarn and it shivers — but the yarn itself stays put. The wiggle (the energy) travels; the yarn doesn't go anywhere.
Feel a K-pop bass drop in your chest: that thump is a sound wave moving energy through the air to you, while the air just jiggles in place.

vocab.meaning: a disturbance that carries energy from place to place without carrying the material along
how many wave cycles pass a point each second
how big a wave's swing is — its height from the middle line

screens.framing: No grade here — just try it. Wrong guesses still tune your instincts.

screens.title: Thinking like a scientist (and a baker)
lines: Every time you tweak a cookie recipe and ask 'did that make them chewier?', you're running an experiment.
Scientists just make it FAIR and write down the evidence — then argue from it. Let's learn the moves.

vocab.meaning: anything in an experiment that can change, like oven temperature or amount of sugar
a test where you change only ONE thing and keep everything else the same
a claim is your answer, evidence is the data behind it, reasoning explains why the data supports the claim

items.prompt: Backyard food chain: rosebush → caterpillar → sparrow → your cat. No grade here — just explore: which one is the PRODUCER that makes its own food?
items.hint: Producers don't eat anything — they capture sunlight.
items.explanation: The rosebush is the producer: it makes food from sunlight. Everything after it is a consumer that eats to get energy.

items.prompt: Let's follow the energy through that backyard food chain together.

steps.text: It starts with the SUN. The rosebush is a producer: it captures sunlight and stores that energy as food (sugar). In a food chain, arrows point the way energy FLOWS.
The caterpillar is a consumer — it can't make food, so it eats the rosebush's leaves to get that stored energy. We draw rosebush → caterpillar, the arrow pointing TO the eater.

check.question: Why does the arrow point toward the caterpillar, not away from it?
options: Because energy flows INTO the thing that eats
Because caterpillars are bigger than leaves

steps.text: The sparrow eats the caterpillar, and your cat eats the sparrow. Each arrow passes energy up the chain: caterpillar → sparrow → cat.
But here's the twist: only about a tenth of the energy makes it to each next level — the rest is used up living and moving. That's why food chains stay short.

check.question: Why are there usually only 4–5 links in a food chain?
options: Energy shrinks at every step, so little is left near the top
The sun runs out of light

steps.text: So energy flows one way: sun → rosebush → caterpillar → sparrow → cat, shrinking each step. Your cat rules the top on the leftovers. 🐱

items.prompt: Your turn — finish tracing this pond food chain: algae → minnow → heron.

lines: Algae is the producer: it makes its own food from [[sunlight]].
The minnow eats the algae, so the energy arrow points to the [[minnow]].
Energy flows one way: algae → minnow → [[heron]].

items.hint: Producers capture light; arrows point toward whatever does the eating.
items.explanation: Energy starts in the producer (algae) and flows up the chain: algae → minnow → heron.

items.prompt: Your cat naps in a backyard full of living and non-living things. Which of these is an ABIOTIC (non-living) part of that ecosystem?
items.hint: Abiotic parts were never alive.
items.explanation: Abiotic means non-living — rocks, water, air, sunlight. The worm, dandelion, and sparrow are all biotic (living).

items.prompt: Sort each part of a pond into living or non-living.
items.hint: If it can grow, eat, or reproduce, it's biotic.
items.explanation: Biotic = living (frog, reed, beetle); abiotic = the non-living surroundings (water, sunlight, mud).

items.prompt: Fill in the three roles every ecosystem needs.

lines: A [[producer]] makes its own food from sunlight.
A [[consumer]] gets energy by eating other living things.
A [[decomposer]] breaks down dead matter and returns nutrients to the soil.

items.hint: Think: the maker, the eater, the recycler.
items.explanation: Producers make food, consumers eat, and decomposers recycle the leftovers back into the soil.

items.prompt: Grass is a producer. What does it use to make its own food?
items.hint: Producers run on light, not on eating.
items.explanation: Through photosynthesis, producers turn sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide into sugar — their food.

items.prompt: Which biome is hot and dry, with cacti and animals that hide from the midday heat?
items.hint: Think of a place with very little rain and lots of sand.
items.explanation: A desert is defined by very low rainfall; its plants and animals are built to save water.

items.prompt: In the Herbology greenhouse, drag each organism into its ecosystem role.
items.hint: Producers make food, consumers eat it, decomposers break down the dead.
items.explanation: The plants (mandrake, geranium) produce; the gnome and flobberworm consume; the fungus and bacteria decompose.

items.prompt: How is a food WEB different from a single food chain?
items.answer: A food web links many food chains, since most animals eat several things and are eaten by several others
options: A food web links many food chains, since most animals eat several things and are eaten by several others
A food web contains only plants
A food web shows energy flowing in a never-ending circle
A food web is just a food chain drawn backwards
items.hint: Real animals rarely eat just one food.
items.explanation: A food web is many overlapping food chains, because organisms usually have several food sources and predators.

items.prompt: Label this meadow food web. Energy starts at the sun.
items.hint: Find the energy source, the plant, the plant-eater, the meat-eater, and the recycler.
items.explanation: Sun → clover (producer) → grasshopper (herbivore) → shrew (carnivore); the mushroom (decomposer) recycles the dead.

items.prompt: Put this ocean food chain in order, starting with the producer.
items.hint: Producers come first; the largest predator is last.
items.explanation: Energy flows phytoplankton → krill → mackerel → seal.

items.prompt: Air is almost four-fifths nitrogen, but plants can't grab it from the sky. What changes nitrogen into a form plant roots can absorb?
items.answer: Bacteria in the soil and on plant roots
options: Bacteria in the soil and on plant roots
Rain washing it off the leaves
items.hint: Tiny living recyclers underground do this job.
items.explanation: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria turn air nitrogen into compounds plants can take up through their roots.

items.prompt: Label this grassland energy pyramid, widest level first.
items.hint: The bottom level makes its own food; energy shrinks going up.
items.explanation: Producers (grasses) hold the most energy; it passes up to grasshopper → lizard → hawk, shrinking about 90% each step.

items.prompt: Two of these statements about energy pyramids are true. Spot the LIE.

truths: Only about 10% of the energy at one level passes up to the next level.
The producer level at the bottom has the most available energy.
data.lie: Top predators have the most energy available to them.

items.explanation: Energy shrinks about 90% at every step, so the top level has the LEAST energy — which is why top predators are rare.

items.prompt: Label this enchanted-forest food web.
items.hint: Trace energy from the sun to the producer, then up to the predators.
items.explanation: Sun → oak (producer) → deer (herbivore) → wolf (carnivore); the toadstool (decomposer) breaks down the dead.

items.prompt: Two of these statements about decomposers are true. Spot the LIE.

truths: Decomposers such as fungi and bacteria break down dead plants and animals.
Decomposers return nutrients to the soil so producers can use them again.
data.lie: A healthy ecosystem doesn't really need decomposers.

items.explanation: Without decomposers, dead matter and nutrients would pile up and never cycle back, and producers would starve — decomposers are essential.

items.prompt: Match each population interaction to an example.

pairs: A cat stalking and catching a mouse
Two oak trees reaching for the same sunlight
A bee feeding on nectar while pollinating a flower
A mushroom breaking down a fallen log

items.hint: Who hunts? Who shares a resource? Who BOTH benefit? Who recycles?
items.explanation: Predation = one hunts another; competition = both need the same resource; mutualism = both benefit; decomposition = breaking down the dead.

items.prompt: Trace water as it cycles through the environment.

lines: The sun heats a lake and water rises as vapor: [[evaporation]].
High up, the vapor cools into cloud droplets: [[condensation]].
The droplets fall back as rain or snow: [[precipitation]].

items.hint: Up as vapor, cool into clouds, fall back down.
items.explanation: Water cycles endlessly: evaporation → condensation → precipitation.

items.prompt: Two of these statements about the carbon cycle are true. Spot the LIE.

truths: A plant builds most of its body from carbon it pulls out of the air as carbon dioxide.
Breathing out (respiration) and decay return carbon to the air as carbon dioxide.
data.lie: Carbon gets used up and disappears as it passes through living things.

items.explanation: Carbon is never destroyed — it cycles: plants capture CO₂, animals eat plants, and respiration and decay release it again.

items.prompt: An energy pyramid starts with 60,000 kcal of energy in the producers. Using the 10% rule, how many kcal reach the SECONDARY consumers (two levels up)?
items.hint: Take 10%, then 10% of that.
items.explanation: 10% of 60,000 = 6,000 at the primary level, and 10% of 6,000 = 600 kcal at the secondary level.

items.prompt: In the wizarding forest's food chain the producers store 10,000 kcal. Using the 10% rule, how many kcal reach the TERTIARY consumers (three levels up)?
items.hint: Drop to a tenth, three times.
items.explanation: 10,000 → 1,000 → 100 → 10 kcal: about 90% is lost at every step, so the top predator gets very little.

items.prompt: A savanna easily feeds thousands of grass-eating zebras but only a few lions. Using the idea that about 90% of energy is lost at each step up a food chain, why?
items.answer: Each level up has far less energy, so the top can support only a few large predators
options: Each level up has far less energy, so the top can support only a few large predators
Zebras reproduce but lions never do
items.hint: Follow the shrinking energy from grass upward.
items.explanation: Only about 10% of energy passes up each step, so by the predator level there is little left — only a few top predators can be fed.

items.prompt: Legendary: an eagle is a tertiary consumer that needs 75 kcal of energy. Using the 10% rule (each level holds about ten times the level above it), at LEAST how many kcal must the producers capture from the sun?
items.hint: Work downward: multiply by 10 for each step from eagle back to the producers — three steps.
items.explanation: Eagle 75 → secondary 750 → primary 7,500 → producers 75,000 kcal. Energy loss means producers must capture far more than the top needs.

items.prompt: No grade — just explore. You pluck one tight strand of knitting yarn and a shiver races to the far end. What does that wave actually carry to the other end?
items.hint: The strand wiggles but stays put — so what made the trip?
items.explanation: A wave carries ENERGY from place to place; the yarn just jiggles and stays where it is.

items.prompt: Let's map the parts of a wave together.

steps.text: Draw a wavy line with a middle resting line through it. The highest point above the middle is the CREST; the lowest point below is the TROUGH.
The distance from one crest to the very next crest is the WAVELENGTH — that's one full cycle of the wave.

check.question: Which part is the lowest point of the wave?

steps.text: How far the wave swings from the middle line up to a crest is the AMPLITUDE. A taller swing means the wave carries MORE energy.
FREQUENCY is how many full waves pass a point each second. Squeeze the waves closer together and more of them go by per second.

check.question: A wave with taller crests (bigger amplitude) carries…?

steps.text: Here's the key link: if the wavelength gets SHORTER, more waves fit in the same space and more pass each second — so the frequency goes UP. Higher frequency means a shorter wavelength.

check.question: If a wave's wavelength gets shorter, its frequency…?

items.prompt: Your turn — fill in the parts of the wave.

lines: The highest point of a wave is the [[crest]]; the lowest point is the trough.
The distance from one crest to the next is the [[wavelength]], and how tall it swings from the middle is the amplitude.
If the wavelength gets shorter, the frequency gets [[higher]].

items.hint: Highest point, crest-to-crest distance, then the wavelength–frequency link.
items.explanation: Crest = highest point, wavelength = crest-to-crest distance, and shorter wavelength means higher frequency.

items.prompt: On a wave, what do we call the highest point?
items.hint: Picture the very top of the wave's hump.
items.explanation: The crest is the highest point of a wave; the matching low point is the trough.

items.prompt: What do we call the LOWEST point of a wave?
items.hint: It's the dip, the opposite of the crest.
items.explanation: The trough is the lowest point of a wave, the opposite of the crest.

items.prompt: Sound is a wave. For a sound wave to reach your ears at a K-pop concert, what does it need to travel through?
items.answer: Something to travel through, like air or water
options: Something to travel through, like air or water
Nothing at all — it travels through empty space
items.hint: Sound has to push on tiny bits of material to move.
items.explanation: Sound needs a medium (a material like air, water, or a solid) to carry it — it cannot travel through empty space.

items.prompt: Two of these statements about water waves are true. Spot the LIE.

truths: A wave carries energy from one place to another.
As a wave passes, the water mostly bobs up and down in place rather than racing along with it.
data.lie: A wave carries the water itself all the way across the ocean.

items.explanation: Waves move ENERGY, not the material — a floating duck just bobs in place as the wave passes underneath.

items.prompt: A plucked guitar string makes this wave shape. Label its parts.
items.hint: Highest point, lowest point, crest-to-crest distance, and the height of the swing.
items.explanation: Crest = top, trough = bottom, wavelength = crest-to-crest distance, amplitude = swing height. Frequency isn't a position, so it's the decoy.

items.prompt: When a K-pop singer hits a really HIGH note, what is true of that sound wave?
items.hint: Pitch — how high or low a note sounds — is set by one wave property.
items.explanation: Pitch is set by frequency: a higher note means a higher-frequency wave. (Loudness is the separate one — that's amplitude.)

items.prompt: Fill in which wave property controls each thing about a sound.

lines: Turn the music up and the sound waves get a bigger [[amplitude]], so it sounds louder.
Sing a higher note and the sound waves get a higher [[frequency]], so the pitch goes up.

items.hint: Loudness pairs with the swing size; pitch pairs with how often waves arrive.
items.explanation: Amplitude controls loudness; frequency controls pitch — two separate dials on a sound wave.

items.prompt: A wizard's wand sends a ripple of light down this wave. Label its parts.
items.hint: The flat middle isn't labelled here — find the top, bottom, the repeat distance, and the swing height.
items.explanation: Crest = top, trough = bottom, wavelength = one full cycle, amplitude = height from the middle. 'Resting line' is the decoy.

items.prompt: Match each wave property to the thing it controls.
items.hint: Amplitude is the energy dial — for sound it sets loudness, for light it sets brightness.
items.explanation: Frequency sets a sound's pitch and wavelength sets light's colour, while amplitude controls loudness for sound and brightness for light.

items.prompt: Order this part of the electromagnetic spectrum from LONGEST wavelength (lowest frequency) to SHORTEST wavelength (highest frequency).
items.hint: Radio waves are the long, low-frequency end; ultraviolet is past the visible end.
items.explanation: Going radio → microwave → infrared → visible → ultraviolet, the wavelength shrinks and the frequency climbs.

items.prompt: White light splits into a rainbow because each colour is a different wavelength. Order the colours from LONGEST wavelength to SHORTEST.
items.hint: Red light has the longest wavelength of the visible colours; violet the shortest.
items.explanation: Colour is just wavelength: red is the longest visible wavelength and violet the shortest, which is the rainbow's order.

items.prompt: Two of these statements about light and sound are true. Spot the LIE.

truths: Light can travel through the empty vacuum of space, which is why sunlight reaches Earth.
Sound needs a material like air or water to travel through.
data.lie: If a star exploded nearby, you would hear a loud boom out in space.

items.explanation: Space is nearly empty, so sound has no material to travel through — space is silent. Light needs no medium, so we still see the explosion.

items.prompt: Pop a straw into a glass of chocolate milk and it looks bent or broken at the surface. Why?
items.answer: Light bends (refracts) as it passes between the milk and the air
options: Light bends (refracts) as it passes between the milk and the air
The straw really snaps in half underwater
The milk dissolves the bottom of the straw
Sound waves push the straw sideways
items.hint: The straw is fine — it's the light's path that changes speed and direction.
items.explanation: Light changes speed and direction (refraction) crossing between water and air, so the submerged part of the straw looks shifted.

items.prompt: Sound travels at different speeds in different materials. In which one would a sound wave travel FASTEST?
items.hint: The more tightly packed the particles, the faster they pass the wave along.
items.explanation: Sound goes fastest in solids, slower in liquids, slowest in gases — and not at all in a vacuum, because its particles are packed tightest in solids.

items.prompt: Legendary: you shout at a canyon wall and hear the echo 2 seconds later. Sound travels about 340 metres each second in air. How far away is the wall, in metres?
items.hint: In 2 seconds the sound goes to the wall AND back — that round trip is the long way.
items.explanation: In 2 s the sound travels 340 × 2 = 680 m round trip, so the wall is half of that: 340 m away.

items.prompt: At a fireworks show you see the bright flash, then hear the BOOM a moment later. Why does the flash arrive first?
items.answer: Light travels much faster than sound, so it reaches you first
options: Light travels much faster than sound, so it reaches you first
The flash happens before the explosion makes any sound
Sound waves are blocked by the dark sky
Your eyes simply react before your ears do
items.hint: Compare the speeds of the two waves racing toward you.
items.explanation: Light travels far faster than sound, so the flash reaches you almost instantly while the slower sound arrives a moment later.

items.prompt: A dog whistle makes a sound so high that cats and dogs hear it but people can't. Compared with a low note a person CAN hear, the whistle's sound wave has…
items.answer: a higher frequency and a shorter wavelength
options: a higher frequency and a shorter wavelength
a lower frequency and a longer wavelength
a bigger amplitude but the same frequency
items.hint: Higher pitch means higher frequency — and remember how frequency and wavelength trade off.
items.explanation: A higher pitch is a higher frequency, and higher frequency always means a shorter wavelength.

items.prompt: Let's build a claim–evidence–reasoning argument about cookies together.

steps.text: Start with a testable question: 'Which makes chewier cookies — brown sugar or white sugar?' You bake two batches changing ONLY the sugar type, keeping amounts, oven temp, and time the same. That's a fair test.

check.question: Why keep everything the same except the sugar?
options: So any difference in chewiness must come from the one thing you changed

steps.text: The CLAIM is your answer to the question. After baking, your claim is: 'The brown-sugar cookies are chewier.'
The EVIDENCE is your data — what you actually measured. Ten tasters rated chewiness: the brown-sugar batch averaged 8 out of 10, the white-sugar batch only 4 out of 10.

check.question: Which of these is EVIDENCE for the claim?
options: The chewiness ratings: brown 8/10 vs white 4/10
Brown sugar is a pretty colour

steps.text: The REASONING explains WHY the evidence supports the claim: brown sugar contains molasses, which holds extra moisture, and moister dough bakes up chewier — so higher chewiness scores make sense.
Put it together: Claim (brown sugar is chewier) + Evidence (8 vs 4) + Reasoning (molasses keeps dough moist) = a strong scientific argument. 🍪

check.question: What does the REASONING add that the evidence alone doesn't?
options: It explains WHY the evidence backs the claim

items.prompt: Your turn — finish this claim–evidence–reasoning about a plant experiment.

lines: We change only ONE thing — the amount of light — and keep water and soil the same, which makes it a [[fair test]].
Our answer to the question is the [[claim]]: plants in more sunlight grow taller.
The measured heights, 20 cm in the sun versus 12 cm in the shade, are our [[evidence]].

items.hint: One-thing-changed = the kind of test; your answer = the C word; your data = the E word.
items.explanation: Changing one variable makes it a fair test; the claim is your answer; the evidence is the measured data that backs it up.

items.prompt: Which question can you actually TEST with an experiment?
items.answer: Do bean plants grow taller when music is played to them?
options: Do bean plants grow taller when music is played to them?
Is jazz the most beautiful kind of music?
items.hint: A testable question can be answered by measuring something, not by opinion.
items.explanation: You can measure plant height with and without music — that's testable. The others are matters of opinion, which experiments can't settle.

items.prompt: You change the type of yarn to test which one knits the warmest scarf. What is the INDEPENDENT variable — the thing YOU change on purpose?
options: The size of the knitting needles
items.hint: The independent variable is the one you deliberately set yourself.
items.explanation: You choose the yarn type, so that's the independent variable; the warmth you measure is the dependent variable.

items.prompt: To run a FAIR test, how many things should you change at one time?
items.hint: If you change several things, you can't tell which one caused the result.
items.explanation: A fair test changes only ONE variable at a time, so any difference must come from that single change.

items.prompt: Match each experiment word to what it means.

pairs: The one thing you change on purpose
What you measure as the result
Something you keep the same to stay fair
A testable prediction you can check

items.hint: One you change, one you measure, ones you keep the same, and your prediction.
items.explanation: Independent = what you change, dependent = what you measure, controlled = kept the same, hypothesis = your testable prediction.

items.prompt: Fill in the variable words for this baking experiment.

lines: We change the baking [[time]] — that's the thing we set on purpose.
We then measure how crispy the cookies are, so the crispiness rating is the [[dependent]] variable.

items.hint: First blank: what you change. Second blank: the kind of variable you measure.
items.explanation: Baking time is what you change (independent); the crispiness you measure is the dependent variable.

items.prompt: An experiment tests how the AMOUNT OF WATER affects how tall sunflowers grow. Sort each part by its role.
items.hint: One thing is changed, one is measured, and several are deliberately kept the same.
items.explanation: You change the water (independent), measure the height (dependent), and keep pot, soil, and sunlight the same (controlled).

items.prompt: Claim: your cat prefers the warm laundry pile over the cold floor. Which EVIDENCE best supports this claim?
items.answer: Over ten days, the cat chose the warm laundry 9 times and the cold floor only once
options: Over ten days, the cat chose the warm laundry 9 times and the cold floor only once
The laundry pile smells nice and clean
You think warm spots are cosy too
items.hint: Evidence is measured data about the actual choice, not a feeling or a guess.
items.explanation: The count of choices (9 warm vs 1 cold) is data that directly supports the claim; the rest are opinions or unrelated facts.

items.prompt: Two of these statements about fair tests are true. Spot the LIE.

truths: In a fair test you change only one variable at a time.
Controlled variables are the conditions you deliberately keep the same.
data.lie: Changing several variables at once makes your results clearer.

items.explanation: If you change several things at once you can't tell which one caused the result — that makes results LESS clear, not clearer.

items.prompt: This plan is meant to be a fair test of a new plant food. One part breaks the fairness — tap it.

segments: To test a new plant food,
she gives Plant A the food and Plant B none,
but she also puts Plant A on a sunny windowsill and Plant B in a dark closet,
then measures how tall each plant grows.

items.hint: Look for a SECOND thing that changed besides the plant food.
items.explanation: She changed two things — the food AND the light — so she can't tell which caused the difference. Keep the light the same for both plants.

items.prompt: A bar graph of plant growth shows: No fertilizer = 5 cm, Low = 9 cm, High = 14 cm. What does the data show?
items.answer: More fertilizer is linked to taller plants
options: More fertilizer is linked to taller plants
Fertilizer has no effect on height
Less fertilizer grows the tallest plants
All three groups grew the same amount
items.hint: Read the bars in order and see which way the heights move.
items.explanation: As the fertilizer goes from none to low to high, the heights rise (5 → 9 → 14 cm), so more fertilizer links to taller plants.

items.prompt: Put the steps of a scientific investigation in the right order.

sequence: Run a fair test and collect data

items.hint: You can't analyse data before you've collected it.
items.explanation: Question → hypothesis → fair test and data → analysis → conclusion is the path of a scientific investigation.

items.prompt: Legendary: a young wizard claims her left-handed wand casts brighter sparks. Which reply is the strongest claim–evidence–reasoning argument?
items.answer: Bright sparks appeared in 9 of 10 left-hand casts but only 3 of 10 right-hand casts, and the left grip lets more magic flow — so the data fits the claim
options: Bright sparks appeared in 9 of 10 left-hand casts but only 3 of 10 right-hand casts, and the left grip lets more magic flow — so the data fits the claim
Left-handed wands are simply better, everyone knows it
I measured the sparks very carefully with a ruler
Lefties are just luckier than right-handers
items.hint: A full argument needs a claim, real measured evidence, AND reasoning that links them.
items.explanation: Only the first reply has all three: a claim, evidence (9/10 vs 3/10), and reasoning explaining why the grip would cause it.

items.prompt: Legendary: this experiment has a hidden design flaw. Tap the part that makes the result untrustworthy.

segments: A gardener tests whether a new plant food works
by feeding it to just ONE plant and comparing with one untreated plant,
keeping the water, light, and soil the same for both,
then measures each plant's height after two weeks.

items.hint: Even with everything controlled, could a single plant's result just be luck?
items.explanation: With only one plant in each group, a difference could be chance — a trustworthy test needs several plants per group (a bigger sample).

items.prompt: Legendary: Amal tests whether warmer water makes bread yeast bubble more. She uses 1 tsp yeast and 1 tsp sugar in EACH cup and changes only the water temperature. Which is a CONTROLLED variable?
items.answer: The amount of sugar — 1 tsp in every cup
options: The amount of sugar — 1 tsp in every cup
The number of bubbles that form
items.hint: A controlled variable is one she keeps exactly the same in every cup.
items.explanation: The sugar is kept the same in every cup, so it's a controlled variable. The temperature is what she changes; the bubbles are what she measures.
